paras: Deloitte has bought its way into another AI business. Its venture arm, D71 Ventures, has acquired the AI business of Flipside Crypto and relaunched it as Edisyl, a new standalone enterprise AI company, Consultancy.org reported on November 13.

Flipside is a Boston-based firm best known for blockchain data and analytics tools for crypto organisations. According to CB Insights, it raised about $65.7 million over seven funding rounds and was valued at $350 million in April 2022.

The deal fits a broader push at Deloitte. Its US arm launched Zora AI, a suite of AI agents, and the firm then set up a Global Agentic Network to build agents for clients. Bloomberg Law reported in September that Deloitte is almost halfway through a five-year commitment to spend $3 billion on AI.

howItWorks.title: How trucking makes money (and why it barely does)
howItWorks.body: Freight is paid by the mile, but trucks often drive back empty. A huge, fragmented market of carriers, brokers in the middle and constant cost pressure means margins are thin.
howItWorks.summary: Running a truck cost a record $2.34 a mile in 2025, according to the industry's main benchmark. Rates have not kept pace, and a sixth of all miles earn nothing. Here is why the economics are so tight.
howItWorks.ai: load matching, route and fuel optimisation, and automated freight brokerage.
howItWorks.caseq: A 200-truck regional carrier makes a 2% margin. The owner wants it doubled in 12 months. What are your levers?

paras: Trucking moves most of the goods in North America, and it is a business of very small margins and very large numbers of players. Shippers (the manufacturers and retailers with goods to move) pay carriers (the companies that own the trucks) by the mile or by the load. Brokers sit between them, matching loads to trucks and keeping a spread.

The basic problem is that the costs are mostly fixed or hard to control, while the price is set by supply and demand in an open market. When there are more trucks than freight, rates fall below what it costs to run them, and carriers keep driving anyway because a parked truck still has a payment due.

A carrier earns revenue per loaded mile, under either a contract with a shipper (a rate agreed for a year or so) or on the spot market (a price for a single load, set daily). Contract rates give stability; spot rates swing with demand and tend to run below costs when the market is weak.

The numbers show how tight things have been. FreightWaves, drawing on ATRI and its own SONAR rate data, reports that contract linehaul rates once cleared carriers' non-fuel costs by about $1.01 per loaded mile in 2022. By 2025 that cushion had shrunk to $0.26. Spot rates sat below non-fuel cost every year from 2023 to 2025. Dry van contract rates averaged $2.69 a mile in the third quarter of 2026, which FreightWaves says is below fourth-quarter 2021 levels, while non-fuel costs are about 30% higher than in 2021. In its view, the 2026 rate rise is a correction rather than a boom.

The industry benchmark is the American Transportation Research Institute's annual survey. Its 2026 edition, covering 2025, put the average cost of operating a truck at $2.336 per mile, up 3.4% and the highest in the report's history. Excluding fuel, costs rose 4.2% to $1.854 per mile.

The main lines: driver wages were about 82 cents per mile, with another 21 cents for benefits. Fuel was about 48 cents. Repair and maintenance rose 8.6% to 21.5 cents. Insurance was 10.6 cents per mile, up 3.9% in a year and 23.9% since 2021. Tariffs pushed tyre costs up 6.4% to about 5 cents. According to ATRI, only fuel and driver pay rose more slowly than inflation.
ATRI's previous report, covering 2024, found operating margins had fallen below 2%. Reading across both reports: a carrier that mismanages a few cents per mile can move from profit to loss.

sections.h: The number that runs the business
paras: The number is the share of miles driven empty. In ATRI's report on 2024 data, empty miles averaged 16.7%. Every empty mile still burns fuel, driver time and tyres but earns nothing.

A simple illustration: if a truck costs $2.34 per mile driven and 16.7% of miles are empty, the cost of each loaded mile is about $2.80 (2.336 divided by 0.833). Pricing a load at $2.50 a mile can therefore lose money even when it looks profitable. This is why carriers fight for backhauls, loads on the return leg, and why dense networks and repeat lanes beat one-off spot freight.

The most developed uses are digital freight matching (software that finds a load for an empty truck), route and fuel optimisation, and automated brokerage that prices and books freight without a phone call. Each of these targets the same issues: empty miles and brokers' spreads.
Autonomous trucks are a longer-term story and are not yet a material part of the economics. The nearer-term win for most fleets is data: knowing their true cost per mile by lane and by customer.

Winners are carriers with dense, repeat freight and low empty miles, those with strong contracts instead of spot exposure, and brokers with better pricing data. Losers are small fleets that cannot absorb a record insurance and maintenance bill.

Industry voices quoted by trade press describe 2026 as a turning point for freight rates, but also say costs are rising fast enough that fleets must keep cutting costs. For consultants, trucking is a clean example of a fragmented industry in which operational detail, not strategy slides, decides who survives.

howItWorks.caseAnswer: Start from the profit equation: margin equals revenue per mile minus cost per mile, divided by revenue per mile, so doubling a 2% margin to 4% needs roughly a 2% improvement in net revenue per mile. Levers, grouped MECE: (1) Revenue: shift mix from spot to contract, reprice the worst 10% of lanes, add accessorial charges (detention, layover), and raise rates on customers where the carrier's service is hard to replace. (2) Utilisation: cut empty miles by lining up backhauls and adding repeat lanes; each point of empty miles is worth about the same as a point of revenue. (3) Cost: fuel efficiency (idle time, speed, tyres), maintenance planning, insurance renegotiation and safety scoring, and driver retention to reduce turnover cost. (4) Overheads and capital: right-size the trailer-to-truck ratio and delay replacing old equipment. Prioritise by size and speed: empty miles and lane repricing first, because they need no capital and show results within a quarter. Validate with a cost-per-loaded-mile model by lane before acting.

howItWorks.title: How Chipotle runs a restaurant
howItWorks.body: Company-owned stores, a short menu and an assembly line built for speed. The economics come down to how many orders each store can push through at the lunch peak.
howItWorks.ai: digital ordering lanes, kitchen automation, and AI tools that tell crews what to cook and when.
howItWorks.caseq: Chipotle wants to raise throughput 10% without adding staff. What are your levers?
howItWorks.summary: Chipotle sells about $3.3 billion of burritos and bowls a quarter from more than 4,100 restaurants it owns itself. Here's how the machine works, where the money goes, and why the whole business comes down to one number: entrées per peak 15 minutes.

paras: Chipotle is a fast-casual chain with a deliberately simple model: a short menu of burritos, bowls, tacos and salads, assembled in front of the customer on a single production line. Unlike McDonald's or Subway, it doesn't franchise. It owns and operates every restaurant it runs in North America and Europe, which means it keeps all of each store's profit, but also carries all of its costs and risks.

That choice shapes everything. A franchisor earns royalties and lets franchisees worry about labour and food costs. Chipotle earns the full margin on every bowl, so its results move directly with how efficiently each restaurant runs. When things go well, the economics are excellent. When costs rise or traffic falls, there's no franchisee to absorb the hit.

Almost all revenue is food and drink sold in its own restaurants. In the third quarter of 2026, total revenue rose 9.6% to $3.3 billion. Most of that growth came from opening new restaurants, with a smaller boost from existing ones: comparable restaurant sales (stores open at least 13 months) rose 2.1%, made up of a 1.3% higher average bill and 0.8% more transactions.

That split matters. Growth from new stores is predictable but capital-hungry. Growth from more customers in existing stores is the healthiest kind, because it spreads fixed costs over more sales. Chipotle had a rough 2025: comparable sales fell 1.7% and customer counts fell 3.2%, its first full-year decline in over 20 years. Q3 2026 was its third straight quarter of rising transactions, which is why investors cheered. The shares jumped about 9% the day after the results.

Digital orders through the app, website and delivery platforms made up 38.8% of food and beverage revenue in the quarter, up from 36.7% a year earlier. Its loyalty programme, relaunched in April, now accounts for over a third of sales.

The key profitability measure is restaurant-level operating margin: revenue minus the direct costs of running restaurants (food, packaging, labour, rent and other operating costs). In Q3 2026 it was 23.3%, down from 24.5% a year earlier.

Where each dollar goes, roughly: food, beverage and packaging took 29.5% of revenue, and labour took 25.7%, up from 25.2% as wages rose. The rest covers occupancy and other operating costs before the margin. Beef and freight costs pushed food costs up, while menu price increases helped offset them.

Each restaurant does about $3.1 million in sales a year on a trailing basis, according to industry tracking of Chipotle's average restaurant sales. New restaurants are a big part of the story: management has said new stores deliver about 60% cash-on-cash returns in their second year, which is why it keeps opening one almost every day.

sections.h: The number that runs the business: throughput
paras: Because Chipotle sells most of its food in a few busy hours, the real constraint isn't demand. It's how many people a restaurant can serve during the lunch and dinner rush. The company measures this as entrées per peak 15 minutes. Every extra entrée served at peak is almost pure profit, because rent, staff and equipment are already paid for.

That's why most of Chipotle's strategy targets speed: a second, dedicated makeline for digital orders; the Chipotlane (a drive-through lane for pre-paid app orders, now in roughly 80% of new restaurants); and a high-efficiency equipment package that it says adds more than two extra entrées during the peak 15 minutes in restaurants that have it.

Chipotle is attacking throughput with a mix of AI and robotics. Its AI-enabled 'Cook to Needs' tool, which forecasts what to cook and when, went from pilot to more than 500 restaurants within the third quarter of 2026.

On the robotics side, it has tested an automated makeline built by Hyphen that assembles bowls and salads for digital orders underneath the counter, and the 'Autocado', which cuts, cores and peels avocados for guacamole. Bowls and salads make up roughly two-thirds of digital orders, which is why automating them could free staff to focus on the front line.

Rivals are racing too: Sweetgreen built its own automated 'Infinite Kitchen', and Cava has invested in Hyphen. For consultants, this is the classic operations question: where does automation raise capacity enough to pay for itself, and where does it just add cost and complexity?

Chipotle's advantages are scale, a simple menu that's easy to run consistently, a strong digital and loyalty base, and the discipline of owning every store. Its risks are the flip side: labour inflation hits it directly, food-safety incidents hurt the whole brand at once, and price increases can push away customers if they go too far.

The next growth chapter is international, with partner-operated restaurants in markets such as Mexico and the Middle East. It lets Chipotle grow abroad without carrying all the risk of building in unfamiliar markets itself. The 2026 plan calls for 350 to 370 new restaurants, including 10 to 15 international partner-operated ones.

howItWorks.caseAnswer: Structure it as capacity per peak 15 minutes = (orders the front line can make + orders the digital line can make) limited by the slowest step. Levers: (1) Labour deployment, not more labour: put the right people on the front line, digital line and grill at peak; the company has shown deployment alone can add several entrées per peak 15 minutes. (2) Remove bottlenecks: prep done before peak (prep failures cascade into slow lines), faster cooking equipment, automated avocado prep. (3) Shift demand: move orders to digital and Chipotlanes, which run in parallel with the front line. (4) Automate the digital line for bowls and salads (about two-thirds of digital orders). (5) Simplify: limit limited-time offers that slow the line. Then size each lever, check payback on equipment, and pilot in a few markets before rolling out.

howItWorks.title: SWOT analysis: how to make four boxes useful
howItWorks.body: Everyone has filled in a SWOT grid. Few people turn it into decisions. Here is how consultants use it, with Chipotle as a worked example.
howItWorks.summary: A SWOT lists strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats. Done badly it is a bland list. Done well it ranks what matters and ends in choices. We apply it to Chipotle, using its latest results.
howItWorks.ai: AI can draft a SWOT in seconds, but the draft is generic. Its best use is gathering evidence for each box, while people do the judging and ranking.
howItWorks.caseq: A regional grocery chain asks you for a SWOT analysis. What do you do before you draw the four boxes?

paras: A SWOT analysis sorts what is true about a business into four boxes. Strengths and weaknesses are internal: things the company controls or can change, like its brand, costs, people and processes. Opportunities and threats are external: things happening in the market that the company does not control, like customer trends, competitors, regulation and input prices.

The framework is popular because it is simple, and that is also its weakness. A grid of generic bullets (strong brand, rising competition) tells a client nothing they did not know. A SWOT earns its place only when every item is specific, backed by a number, ranked by importance, and connected to a decision.

Start with a question, not a grid. A SWOT of the whole company is rarely useful; a SWOT for a decision, such as whether to open in a new country or add automation, is. The question decides which facts matter.

Then use one test to sort every item: could the company change it next year? If yes, it is internal (a strength or weakness). If no, it is external (an opportunity or threat). Most mistakes come from putting an outside trend, like rising wages, into the weakness box.

Attach evidence to every bullet: a figure, a date and a source. Then rank each box by two things, how much it could move the results and how likely it is. Keep the top three or four in each box and drop the rest.

Chipotle's third-quarter 2026 results give plenty of evidence. Strengths: it owns all of its restaurants in North America, so it keeps the whole margin (23.3% restaurant-level margin in the quarter); digital orders are 38.8% of food and beverage sales; and its loyalty programme accounts for more than a third of sales. Its design is built around throughput, serving more people in the lunch rush.

Weaknesses: that same ownership means no franchisee to absorb cost increases. Margin fell from 24.5% to 23.3% in a year, and labour rose to 25.7% of revenue from 25.2%. The business also had a poor 2025, with comparable sales down 1.7% and customer counts down 3.2%, so it is recovering rather than cruising.

Opportunities: roughly 350 to 370 new restaurants planned for 2026, including 10 to 15 international partner-operated ones; drive-through Chipotlanes in about 80% of new restaurants; and automation such as the Cook to Needs forecasting tool, already in more than 500 restaurants, plus the robotic makeline and avocado machine being tested.

Threats: a food-safety incident would hit the whole brand at once; beef and freight costs push up food costs; further price increases could push customers away; and rivals such as Sweetgreen and Cava are building their own automation.

The step most people skip is turning the grid into strategy. A common method is a TOWS matrix, which crosses the boxes: use strengths to seize opportunities, use strengths to blunt threats, fix weaknesses that block opportunities, and protect against the combination of weaknesses and threats.

For Chipotle: its strong throughput and digital base (strengths) support rapid rollout of Chipotlanes in new stores (opportunity). Its exposure to labour inflation (weakness) is the reason automation (opportunity) matters. Its single-brand risk (threat) argues for a very high food-safety standard. Each crossing becomes a candidate strategy, which you then rank and assign an owner.
The deliverable is not the grid. It is a short list of prioritised moves, each tied to evidence.

The usual failures are generic bullets with no numbers, mixing internal and external factors, listing 20 items per box, treating every item as equal, and stopping at the list. A related error is using a SWOT as the whole analysis: it organises facts but does not size markets, test economics or compare options. It works best as a summary step after real research.

Another trap is looking only at the company's own point of view. A strength matters only relative to competitors: a loyal customer base is a strength if rivals lack one, and table stakes if they all have it.

AI tools will draft a SWOT in seconds, and the result is usually fluent but generic. Their useful role is evidence gathering: pulling figures from filings, summarising earnings calls and spotting competitor moves. The judgment, which items matter and what to do about them, is still the consultant's job, and it is where the value is.

howItWorks.caseAnswer: Before drawing anything, clarify the decision the client faces (for example, whether to fund a new format, enter a new region or cut costs) because that determines scope. Then gather evidence in three streams: internal data (store-level margins, shrink, labour cost, loyalty data), customer research (price perception, share of basket), and the market (competitor openings, discounters, supplier inflation, local regulation). Build the SWOT only after that, with every bullet carrying a number and a source and tested as internal or external. Rank by impact and likelihood, keep the top three per box, and cross them in a TOWS matrix to generate options. Present three to five prioritised strategic moves with owners, quick wins first, and note which assumptions need testing. Finally, challenge it: which strengths are real relative to competitors, and what would change the ranking?

policy.title: EU pushes its toughest AI Act rules back to December 2027
policy.summary: Lawmakers agreed to delay the AI Act's high-risk obligations by about 16 months. The delay changes when companies must spend on compliance, not whether they must comply.
policy.cs: Banks, insurers, HR-tech and health clients get more time, but still need AI inventories, risk classification and governance programmes. Expect work to be re-phased, not cancelled.

dates.label: EU AI Act: high-risk obligations for stand-alone AI systems apply
EU AI Act: high-risk obligations for AI embedded in regulated products apply

paras: The European Union has agreed to postpone the most demanding parts of its AI Act. Under the Digital Omnibus on AI, obligations for high-risk systems that stand alone now apply from 2 December 2027 instead of 2 August 2026. Rules for high-risk AI built into regulated products, such as machinery, move to 2 August 2028, according to law-firm summaries of the agreement.

High-risk systems are the ones used in areas such as hiring, education, credit and insurance, law enforcement, biometrics and critical infrastructure. The delay was justified by missing technical standards and guidance: companies argued they could not comply with rules that did not yet have a rulebook behind them. The European Commission first proposed the change in November 2025, and Parliament and the Council reached a deal in 2026.

The deal is narrower than the headline suggests. Practitioner analysis notes that the bans on certain AI practices (in force since February 2025) and the rules for general-purpose models (since August 2025) were not touched, and that transparency duties in Article 50 still apply from August 2026. The Omnibus mostly streamlines and clarifies the existing text rather than rewriting its risk-based structure.

For clients, the practical point is timing. Teams that use the extra months to build inventories of their AI systems, classify them by risk and set up governance will be ahead of the queue for conformity assessments in 2027. Those that treat the delay as a cancellation will face a compressed deadline later.
unknowns: Whether every detail of the agreed text has completed formal adoption.
How quickly the harmonised technical standards will actually be published.

policy.title: Canada's AI plan: big spending, no AI law, new privacy and online-safety bills
policy.summary: Ottawa's AI for All strategy leans on privacy reform and online-safety legislation instead of a dedicated AI act, and adds a trusted-AI certification scheme and sovereign data-centre plans.
policy.cs: Canadian clients face privacy and data-governance obligations first, not an AI-specific regime. Demand: privacy programmes, AI governance and assurance, and sovereign-compute strategy.
paras: Prime Minister Mark Carney and AI Minister Evan Solomon launched Canada's national AI strategy, AI for All, on 4 June 2026. It proposes large-scale data centres, a sovereign AI foundation and measures to attract foreign investment into Canadian AI, and a Canada Trusted AI Certification programme to identify trustworthy products in the market.

The notable choice is what it leaves out. Law-firm and commentary analysis agrees that the government does not plan AI-specific regulation. Instead it relies on updating privacy law and bringing back online-safety legislation, a different path from the EU's dedicated AI Act. An earlier federal bill with AI rules, the Artificial Intelligence and Data Act, died with the previous Parliament, and commentators note the government does not appear to intend to reintroduce AI-specific legislation.

Parliament now has a set of related bills. Solomon tabled a long-awaited private-sector privacy bill with stiff fines in June, and the government has also tabled the Safe Social Media Act, which would create a Digital Safety Act. Solomon has said he is confident the bills together will protect children, personal information and privacy.

Critics, including law professor Michael Geist, have called the strategy big on spending but short on the specifics that matter, such as transparency requirements. For Canadian companies the message is to prepare for stronger privacy duties, and to expect certification and procurement rules to shape which AI products public bodies buy.
unknowns: When the privacy and online-safety bills will pass, and in what form.

policy.title: Washington's push to override state AI laws: what the order does and doesn't do
policy.summary: A December 2025 executive order set up a Justice Department task force to challenge state AI laws. The order alone doesn't cancel them, so companies still have to comply with state rules.
policy.cs: Multi-state clients need a compliance plan that works under both outcomes: state rules stay, or a federal standard replaces them. Scenario planning and regulatory monitoring are the work.
paras: On 11 December 2025 President Trump signed an executive order titled Ensuring a National Policy Framework for Artificial Intelligence. It directs the Attorney General to create an AI Litigation Task Force whose job is to challenge state AI laws, on grounds such as interference with interstate commerce or conflict with federal law. The Commerce Department was told to review state AI laws and refer potentially unlawful provisions to the task force, with a list due in March 2026.

The order also asks White House advisers to draft a legislative proposal for a single federal framework that would override conflicting state laws, while carving out areas such as child safety, data-centre infrastructure and state government use of AI. It singled out Colorado's algorithmic-discrimination law as an early target.

Legal analysts stress the limits. An executive order is not a statute, so on its own it does not displace state law. Until courts invalidate a state rule, companies must keep complying with it. A February 2026 analysis notes that Colorado's AI Act (effective 30 June 2026) and California's frontier-AI transparency law (effective 1 January 2026) were unlikely to be affected in the short term.

The order has drawn criticism from labour groups and from politicians in both parties, and support from some policy analysts who want a single national standard. For clients that operate across states, the practical task is to build compliance that survives either result.
unknowns: How the courts will rule on any federal challenge to a state AI law.
Whether Congress passes a federal framework, and what it would preempt.
The current status of Colorado's start date: we have not re-checked it since the February 2026 analysis cited here.

deskNews.title: PNC lets corporate clients get paid in USDC, with Coinbase handling the stablecoin leg
deskNews.summary: PNC says eligible corporate and institutional clients can now receive USDC on Ethereum, converted one-to-one into dollars in their PNC accounts. It is a receive-only service, but it puts a large US bank on stablecoin rails.
deskNews.cs: Treasury, payments and cash-management teams at banks now have a live peer to benchmark against. Expect client work on stablecoin operating models: custody, reconciliation, fraud and liquidity, rather than whether to engage at all.
paras: PNC announced on 9 November that clients in its Corporate and Institutional Banking unit can receive payments in USDC, a dollar-backed stablecoin, on the Ethereum network. Coinbase's payment products run the stablecoin side, while PNC provides the deposit account and treasury services.

The structure matters more than the headline. Funds arrive as USDC but are converted automatically at one-to-one into US dollars, so the client sees a bank balance rather than a crypto position. That keeps accounting, tax and risk treatment close to what the client already does.

For consultants, the pattern is a bank renting specialist infrastructure instead of building it. The open questions are economics (who earns the fee on conversion), controls (sanctions and fraud screening on-chain) and scope: this is incoming payments only.
questions: Is this a revenue line or a defensive move for the bank's payments franchise?
What controls sit between an on-chain deposit and a bank balance?
Which of our clients' counterparties already pay in stablecoins?
unknowns: Pricing and fees were not part of the announcement.
Whether outgoing payments are planned.

deskNews.title: Stablecoin payments reach about $482 billion in nine months as card networks and banks plug in
deskNews.summary: One analytics firm counts roughly $482 billion of stablecoin payments in the first nine months of 2026, up 45% on a year earlier. Mastercard, Visa and Stripe are all building products that connect stablecoins to ordinary payments.
deskNews.cs: Payments strategy is moving from 'will stablecoins matter' to 'where do we sit in the chain'. Banks, processors and large merchants will want help choosing between building, partnering and staying out.
paras: Figures reported this month attribute the $482 billion payments total and 45% growth to Allium, a blockchain analytics firm. The same coverage says Mastercard launched a platform that combines fiat and stablecoin balances, and Stripe partnered with the Plasma network on cards that span currencies.

Trackers put the overall stablecoin market at roughly $280 billion at the start of September, though the number depends on methodology. Separately, Coinbase received conditional approval in April for a national trust bank charter from the US Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, a sign regulators are bringing stablecoin infrastructure inside the banking perimeter.

Treat the payments total with care: analytics firms define 'payments' differently and some volume is trading activity. The direction of travel, incumbents wrapping stablecoins rather than fighting them, is better supported than the exact number.
questions: How much of the volume is real commerce versus trading and treasury movement?
Which layer captures the margin: issuer, network, bank or wallet?
What does a bank's compliance model look like when settlement is on-chain?
unknowns: The payments figure comes from one analytics firm reported by an aggregator; we could not check the method.
Share of volume that is consumer or business payments.

deskNews.title: Blackstone and four Canadian pension funds buy into LNG Canada through Mitsubishi's stake
deskNews.summary: A Blackstone-led group will invest US$3.1 billion for 49.9% of the Mitsubishi subsidiary that holds a 15% interest in LNG Canada. The cash helps fund the Phase 2 expansion that doubles the Kitimat terminal.
deskNews.cs: Infrastructure capital is now financing LNG build-out alongside the majors. Expect work on partner capital structures, offtake contracting and construction-cost control as Phase 2 proceeds.
paras: Blackstone Credit and Insurance, with CPP Investments, OMERS, IMCO and PSP, signed the deal on 2 November. Mitsubishi stays the controlling partner and keeps its LNG offtake, about 2.1 million tonnes a year now and 4.2 million after expansion. Reuters reports Mitsubishi values the interest being sold at about US$1.6 billion, with the rest of the investment aimed at Phase 2.

LNG Canada, led by Shell with PetroChina, Petronas, Mitsubishi and KOGAS as partners, began production in June 2025. The partners approved Phase 2 in September 2026, which lifts capacity from roughly 14 to 28 million tonnes a year. Mitsubishi says the deal is expected to close in November.

The structure is the story: a trading house sells a minority stake in a holding company to recycle capital while keeping control and its gas. It is a template other Asian buyers with large project stakes could follow.
questions: What is the return profile for infrastructure credit in an LNG project?
Does Phase 2 stay on budget and schedule?
Which other partners will recycle capital the same way?
unknowns: Terms and pricing beyond the headline amount.
Regulatory approvals still needed to close.

deskNews.title: Oil drops sharply on signs of US–Iran talks, but supply risk through Hormuz remains
deskNews.summary: Crude fell roughly 6 to 7% at its lowest point in the week to 6 November after Iran signalled openness to negotiations, then recovered part of the loss. Prices had been elevated for months on disruption to Middle East supply.
deskNews.cs: Energy clients are planning against a wide price range. Scenario planning, hedging policy and capital-allocation reviews are where this volatility turns into work.
paras: Weekly market summaries describe a volatile week in which oil dropped on hopes of a diplomatic route out of the conflict, with the decline measured at about 6% by one outlet and 7% by another at the low. The summary also notes months of elevated prices tied to uncertainty over the Strait of Hormuz and damaged Gulf infrastructure.

The International Energy Agency separately warned that natural gas markets could stay constrained into 2027 even as LNG and renewables investment grows. That fits the capital flowing into projects such as LNG Canada.
A one-week move on peace headlines says little about the trend. What matters for planning is the spread between a deal scenario and a prolonged disruption.

facts.v: Months of elevated prices; Hormuz uncertainty

questions: What price range should the capital plan survive?
Which projects only work if disruption persists?
How exposed is our supply chain to Gulf shipping?
unknowns: Whether talks lead to an agreement.
Exact closing prices, which vary by benchmark and day.

deskNews.title: OPEC+ holds December output steady; the war, not the quota table, sets real supply
deskNews.summary: Seven core OPEC+ producers kept December production targets unchanged and set their next meeting for 29 November. A capacity review that feeds 2027 quotas has slipped to mid-November.
deskNews.cs: Quota decisions are secondary while actual output is constrained. Clients in oil, refining and petrochemicals need planning that does not assume a return to pre-war supply.
paras: The group said it would keep monthly meetings, with the next on 29 November. A report on the October meeting noted the core members were still pumping about 5 million barrels a day below pre-war levels because of the Iran war, so targets above actual output are largely theoretical.
The capacity review matters because it will shape how quotas are divided in 2027. Delays keep the market guessing about who gets to produce more when supply normalises.
US data released on 4 November put commercial crude stocks, excluding the strategic reserve, at 409.8 million barrels for the week ending 30 October.

facts.k: US commercial crude stocks, wk to Oct 30

questions: When does actual supply recover, and who benefits first?
How will 2027 quotas be allocated after the capacity review?
unknowns: Outcome and timing of the capacity review.

sources.src: Oil Market Daily via PR Newswire

dates.label: OPEC+ core members' next monthly meeting

deskNews.title: Retailers report into a forecast of a $1 trillion holiday season, the fastest growth since 2021
deskNews.summary: The National Retail Federation expects November and December sales to rise 4.2% to $1.013 trillion. Home Depot, Target, Walmart and others report next week, giving the first read on how that holds up against budget-conscious shoppers.
deskNews.cs: Retail clients will be re-planning inventory, pricing and promotions in real time. Watch guidance language on discretionary categories and low-income shoppers.
paras: NRF released the forecast on 15 October, built with Oxford Economics. Last year holiday sales rose 3.1% to $972 billion, below NRF's own range. It says nearly half of this year's growth is real spending and the rest is higher prices, and that growth would be the fastest since 2021.
Earnings land in a tight window: Home Depot on 17 November, Target on 18 November, Walmart and Ross on 19 November and Best Buy on 24 November. Lowe's lists 18 November as tentative.
The forecast is nominal and covers retail excluding autos, gas stations and restaurants, so it will not map neatly onto any single company's results.
questions: Is growth broad or driven by higher-income households?
How much of sales growth is price versus volume?
Where are retailers cutting or adding promotions?
unknowns: Company guidance for the holiday quarter.
Earnings dates other than those the companies have confirmed.

deskNews.title: Best Buy's new CEO starts as the retailer leans on marketplace and retail media
deskNews.summary: Jason Bonfig took over from Corie Barry on 31 October. He built Best Buy's US online marketplace and scaled its retail media business, the two areas the company is counting on for margin.
deskNews.cs: A CEO change at a flat-growth retailer usually precedes a strategy reset. Look for portfolio, store-footprint and margin-mix work after the 24 November earnings call.
paras: Best Buy announced the succession in April. Barry stepped down after seven years and stays as an adviser for six months. Bonfig, a 25-year veteran, oversaw merchandising, e-commerce, marketing, supply chain, Best Buy Canada and the Best Buy Ads network.

The company reported US$41.7 billion of revenue in fiscal 2026, with fourth-quarter comparable sales down 0.8%. Retail media and marketplace are the higher-margin lines the new CEO is known for building.

facts.v: Corie Barry (CEO since 2019), adviser for 6 months

questions: How large can retail media and marketplace get relative to hardware margins?
What does the store network look like in three years?
unknowns: Any strategy changes; the first call under Bonfig is 24 November.

deskNews.title: Medicare's GLP-1 Bridge puts a $50 copay on weight-loss drugs until the end of 2027
deskNews.summary: Since 1 July, eligible Part D members can fill covered obesity drugs for a flat $50 a month under a temporary CMS demonstration. It runs to 31 December 2027, with a longer-term model for Part D planned from 2027.
deskNews.cs: Payers, pharmacies and manufacturers are modelling uptake, prior-authorization workload and plan bids. The sunset date creates a clear planning cliff.
paras: CMS says the Bridge covers Wegovy (injection and tablet), the Zepbound KwikPen and Foundayo for weight loss or weight maintenance. The copay is a flat $50 for a 30-day supply regardless of dose, applies nationwide, and sits outside the normal Part D benefit for the length of the demonstration.

There are limits. People already getting a GLP-1 under Part D for conditions such as type 2 diabetes or sleep apnea are not eligible, the copay does not count toward the deductible or out-of-pocket cap, and Extra Help amounts do not apply. Early reports described pharmacy denials in the first days.

A separate CMS model, announced in December 2025, would let Part D plans and state Medicaid programs cover GLP-1s at negotiated prices, with Part D participation from January 2027 and voluntary for manufacturers, states and plans.

facts.v: CMS BALANCE model; Part D from Jan 2027 (voluntary)

questions: How many eligible members will actually use the benefit?
What happens to coverage when the Bridge ends?
How do plan bids and rebates adjust?
unknowns: Uptake and spend data since July.
Final design of the longer-term model.

deskNews.title: Rail merger fight enters its comment round, with critics backing a bid to end the review
deskNews.summary: Opening comments on Union Pacific's proposed purchase of Norfolk Southern are due 18 November. Shippers critical of the deal have backed Canadian Pacific Kansas City's request that the Surface Transportation Board terminate the review.
deskNews.cs: A five-month comment window is when opponents and shippers build their evidence. Expect heavy demand for competition economics, network modelling and shipper impact analysis.
paras: The STB restarted the proceeding on 18 August and set the schedule: comments, protests and requests for conditions are due 18 November, and responses on 16 February 2027. A public hearing is planned before final briefs, with dates to be set. On 18 September the Board unanimously rejected motions for summary denial from BNSF, CSX and shipper groups, while one member wrote that the applicants still have a long way to go.

On 9 November, MLex reported that critics backed a CPKC request to end the review, arguing public statements by Union Pacific's CEO at a shippers' conference had corrupted the record. The Board has not ruled on that request, and nothing in the schedule has changed.
The competitive question centres on a pricing commitment Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern offered, which BNSF says covers under 1% of rail traffic.

facts.v: CPKC motion to end review, backed by shippers

questions: Which shippers lose rail-to-rail competition?
What conditions could make the deal approvable?
How long does the timetable push closing?
unknowns: Whether the STB acts on the termination request.
Dates of the public hearing.

deskNews.title: Detroit's Big Three line up US plant investments as 25% vehicle tariffs bite
deskNews.summary: The White House points to US manufacturing commitments from GM, Ford and Stellantis as proof tariffs are pulling production home. The investments are real announcements, but the causal claim is the administration's.
deskNews.cs: Auto and supplier clients face footprint decisions: where to build, what to localise and how to price tariff cost. Moves are shifting production between existing plants more than adding capacity.
paras: A July White House release lists GM investing US$6 billion in US manufacturing including an Orion Township expansion, Ford putting US$3 billion into its BlueOval Battery Park in Marshall (1,700 jobs), and Stellantis spending US$388 million on a Van Buren Township hub plus smaller Detroit and Warren projects. The President cited the same investments in Michigan on 29 July.
The policy backdrop is a 25% tariff on vehicles and light trucks built outside the US, plus extended tariffs on foreign-built medium and heavy trucks and an offset for parts on US-built vehicles.

US$3B BlueOval Battery Park (Marshall, MI); 1,700 jobs

25% on foreign-built vehicles and light trucks

deskNews.title: Corus completes its recapitalisation as lenders take ownership and a new board is named
deskNews.summary: Corus has closed the debt-for-equity restructuring after Canadian regulators approved it and Quebecor's rival bid was rejected. The company says it owns 25 specialty channels, 15 conventional stations and 36 radio stations.
deskNews.cs: A restructured balance sheet does not fix the business model. Expect cost programmes, portfolio sales and distribution renegotiations; these are advisory and operations-improvement opportunities.
paras: The deal, first announced in November 2025, was approved by an Ontario court in March 2026 and by the CRTC afterwards. The CRTC also rejected Quebecor's attempt to buy Corus. Closing on 8 October brought in a new board.

The pressure on the business has not eased. In August Corus cut more jobs across Global News and its radio operations, and unions have criticised new job losses at Bell Media and Corus while federal support for Canadian news remains unsettled.
questions: Which assets are core after the restructuring?
How far can costs fall before the content quality suffers?
What happens to carriage deals with cable and streaming?
unknowns: The new owners' plans for assets.

deskNews.title: Ottawa details $600 million in media funding for 2026–27; critics question who pays
deskNews.summary: Heritage Minister Marc Miller broke the money into the Canada Media Fund, local news, Telefilm and music funds. The announcement does not say how much goes to each company.
deskNews.cs: Broadcasters and producers will be modelling how these funds and the proposed journalism tax credit change their economics. Policy and funding-strategy work follows.
paras: On 8 November the government set out the 2026–27 allocation: Canada Media Fund $213.4 million, the Independent Local News Fund $80 million, Telefilm Canada $68.5 million and the Canada Music Fund $67 million. It is separate from a proposed journalism tax-credit expansion in Budget 2026.

Law professor Michael Geist argued taxpayers are covering costs that large technology platforms should bear, citing roughly $1.5 billion across several cultural and news measures. That figure is his tally of wider measures, not payments under this package.
Unions say uncertainty over federal support is pushing news job cuts at Bell Media and Corus.
questions: Who gets what, and under which conditions?
Does the funding offset the loss of platform contributions?
unknowns: Company-by-company allocations.
Currency of the amounts, which the report does not label.

deskNews.title: Strategy firms keep growing but not evenly: BCG up 7%, McKinsey's headcount shrinks, Accenture adds people
deskNews.summary: BCG closed the year at US$14.4 billion, up 7% for a 22nd straight year of growth. At McKinsey, headcount went down for the first time in years, while Accenture ended fiscal 2026 with about 814,000 people.
deskNews.cs: Firm leaders are re-cutting pyramids and pricing. For students and early-career candidates, the entry-level squeeze is the headline.
paras: An industry review notes only BCG discloses revenue among the strategy firms, so comparisons rely on estimates. Revenue kept growing through 2025 across the big firms, but McKinsey's headcount falling was a break from the pattern.

Accenture is often grouped with the Big Four but is not one of them. It reported about 814,000 people at the end of fiscal 2026 versus about 779,000 a year earlier, and Deloitte says it has nearly 500,000. At the Big Four, tax grew faster than advisory: PwC's advisory revenue rose 3.0% like-for-like versus 6.3% for tax and legal.
The same review says Bain bought a London financial-crime compliance firm, JJC FinTech, in February 2026.
questions: Where is demand growing: strategy, implementation or tax?
What does a smaller McKinsey pyramid mean for entry hiring?
unknowns: Non-disclosed firms' revenue.
Which figures are estimates.

deskNews.title: AI is pushing the big firms toward outcome-based fees and expert-heavy teams
deskNews.summary: McKinsey said in November 2025 that about one in four of its global fees now depend on outcomes rather than hours. Bloomberg reported in August that McKinsey, BCG and Bain are emphasising deep technical and industry expertise as AI changes the talent model.
deskNews.cs: If AI compresses analytical hours, pricing tied to hours loses its logic. Firms and clients are renegotiating scope, risk-sharing and value metrics.
paras: McKinsey's UK managing partner, Michael Birshan, told reporters in London that the firm is doing more performance-based work, per Business Insider. That fee mix figure is from late 2025, so check for updates.

The shift matters for the pyramid. If tools handle first-pass analysis, firms need fewer junior analysts per project and more people with deep domain skills. Bain also moved ahead of BCG into second place in Vault's 2026 North American prestige ranking, a rare change at the top.

facts.v: Technical and industry experts over generalists

unknowns: Current fee mix; the share is from late 2025.
